new_statements.quote: Accent is one of the things that was poorly recorded. This makes it difficult to understand the Tutelo accentual pattern. The following comments make best use of the available accentual data and probably represent all that can be said about accent in Tutelo. A lot of Tutelo words, including inflected forms, are accented on the second syllable counting from the beginning of the word. This pattern being typical of Siouan languages, it can be assumed that, at least at one time, this second syllable accentual pattern was the rule in Tutelo. However, several phenomena have modified this original second syllable accentual pattern.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the second syllable counted from the left edge of the word (the pan-Siouan pattern), in the majority of recorded words including inflected forms; the author treats this as the original rule, now obscured by (a) loss of the unaccented first-syllable vowel in some disyllabic verb stems, leaving accented monosyllabic stems that keep their accent under inflection, and (b) inherently accented grammatical morphemes (á- 'locative, on', -ǫ́: 'progressive', -pú '2 plural') that attract the accent and shift or delete the accent of other morphemes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described by Oliverio or Roberts. Sapir 1913 (A Tutelo Vocabulary, p. 297) marks 'main stress' and 'secondary stress' on individual words in his ~50-word list but states no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Oliverio pp. 55-56: monosyllabic accented verb stems from vowel deletion; inherently accented affixes/clitics á-, -ǫ́:, -pú take the accent; p. 121: in reduplicated stative verbs (plural) accent falls on the second of the identical syllables; distributive numerals: suffix -lale shifts the numeral's accent to the syllable immediately preceding it; Hale 1883 p. 30: imperative marked by 'a sharp accent on the final syllable of the verb'; Hale p. 35: accent of lihiok varies with position in the sentence. Roberts 2020 pp. 33-34 repeats the same picture ('stress in the majority of words... falls on the second syllable', inherently accented clitics /ˈa/, /ˈõ:/, /ˈpu/).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word including inflectional affixes and clitics), based on a philological reconstitution of 19th/early-20th-c. transcriptions; the author stresses that accent was poorly recorded and marks accent in the dictionary only where evidence suffices (p. 174). Roberts 2020 (p. 22 n.9) adds that tone was not recorded in the documentation.
new_statements.identity_note: Oliverio 1996 describes Tutelo proper (tute1247) from the 19th/early-20th-century Six Nations records (Hale, Dorsey, Hewitt, Sapir, Frachtenberg); Roberts 2020/2025 use the revitalization name "Tutelo-Saponi" / Yesa:sahį for the same corpus (Saponi is a separate Glottolog languoid, sapo1241, but Roberts' data are the Tutelo records). No dialect split is described.

sources.citation: Roberts, Corey. 2020. A Grammar Sketch of Tutelo-Saponi. MA thesis, University of Arizona. 78 pp. (Glottolog 589260)
sources.note: §2.4 Stress pp. 33-34: 'Unfortunately, stress has not been well documented in the corpus of Tutelo-Saponi. The data available reveal, however, that the stress in the majority of words in the language falls on the second syllable. This is in keeping with the accent pattern typical across Siouan languages.' Exceptions from vowel deletion and inherently accented clitics /ˈa/ 'on', /ˈõ:/ progressive, /ˈpu/ 2pl; p. 22 n.9 tone not recorded; orthography marks stress with acute accent following Oliverio 1996. Derivative of Oliverio.

sources.note: Only remark: in plural reduplicated adjectives 'the accented syllable of the adjective is reduplicated and then in the plural form the second of the two similar syllables is accented' (p. 3).

sources.citation: Hale, Horatio. 1883. The Tutelo Tribe and Language. Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 21(114): 1-47. (Glottolog 662393; reprinted 2001 Evolution Publishing, Glottolog 128159)
sources.note: p. 15 (alphabet): diacritics written only on 'the accented syllable — that is, the syllable on which the stress of voice falls'; no positional rule given. p. 30: imperative 'distinguished apparently by a sharp accent on the final syllable of the verb'. p. 35: 'the accent or stress of voice in the word lihiok, if he comes, appears to vary with the position of the word in the sentence.'

sources.citation: Roberts, Corey. 2025. Verbs and Community: Topics in Tutelo Revitalization. PhD dissertation, University of Arizona. 200 pp.
sources.note: No phonology chapter; p. 46 mentions in passing 'the natural stress in Tutelo falling on the second syllable'; p. 44 says the acute accent in the sources may variously mark length and/or tone and cannot be tied to a phonemic distinction; imperative described via Hale's 'sharp accent on the final syllable' and Oliverio's suffix -í (1996:118). fetched sources from the public Google Drive link posted on yesasahin.org.
